text: A psalm of David. The LORD says to my Lord: "Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet."
The LORD will extend your mighty scepter from Zion. Rule in the midst of your enemies!

versions.text: The LORD will extend your mighty scepter from Zion: rule in the midst of your enemies.
versions.explanation: The colon awkwardly joins a statement to a direct command. A full stop plus an imperative sentence marks the shift in voice more clearly for a reader speaking the line aloud.

text: Your people offer themselves freely on the day of your power; arrayed in holy splendor, from the womb of the dawn, yours is the dew of youth.
The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind: "You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek."
The Lord is at your right hand; he shatters kings on the day of his wrath.
He will judge among the nations, heaping up corpses; he will shatter the head over the wide earth.

versions.text: He will judge among the nations, filling the field with corpses; he will shatter the head over all the wide earth.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has only "filled with corpses" (מָלֵא גְוִיּוֹת) with no noun for "field"; the added object is interpretive. A rendering without supplying an unstated noun stays closer to the text and reads well aloud.

versions.text: He will judge among the nations, heaping up the corpses; he will shatter the head over all the wide earth.
versions.explanation: Two small additions to the Hebrew: גְוִיּוֹת is indefinite ("corpses," not "the corpses"), and עַל־אֶרֶץ רַבָּה is "over the wide earth" with no word corresponding to "all." Removing both keeps the line closer to the text and tightens the rhythm for reading aloud, in line with the earlier decision not to supply unstated words.

text: He will drink from the brook beside the way; therefore he will lift up his head.
